title: Test git fixtures can write into the real .git/config and brick the main working tree
description:
On 2026-08-26 the main working tree of this repo became unusable: git status/add/commit all failed with "fatal: this operation must be run in a work tree". Four values had appeared in .git/config at 13:44 - core.bare=true (the breaking one), user.email=test@example.com, user.name=Test, commit.gpgsign=false. Ryan repaired it by hand. No commit was authored with the bad identity.

The three identity values are byte-identical to _git_init() at tests/test_gitstage.py:47-49 and tests/test_cli.py:2495-2497, which shell out to real git to build a throwaway repo in tmp_path. core.bare=true is the signature of `git init` resolving to the main .git with no work tree.

The carrier is worktree sharing: a linked worktree shares .git/config with the main repo, so a plain `git config <k> <v>` from inside .claude/worktrees/<agent> defaults to --local and writes the COMMON config. The damage was done by worktree agent-a615c1063024add25 on branch seeds-ww8/guard-mixed-stage-flush at 13:44; that work merged as 00ed416 at 13:50 and the worktree was removed at 13:54.

This is a standing hazard, not a one-off: every /bead-go run operates in such a worktree, and any test that shells out to git can repeat it. Blast radius is the developer's main working tree.

Note the irony driving the priority: src/seeds/gitstage.py already has _subprocess_env(), which strips six repo-pinning GIT_* vars, and its comment says it was written after finding this same bug class. The guard landed six minutes AFTER the damage. The guard is correct; what is missing is a detector and positive containment. The repo sat bricked ~20 minutes and was found only when an unrelated `git add` failed.

Deliberation: seed seeds-ngez.
design:
1. DETECT (highest value). Pre-commit assertion that fails loudly when core.bare is true or user.email matches a test fixture. The entire cost here was that a config error surfaces as an unrelated, unexplained git failure. Must run inside worktrees too.

2. CONTAIN POSITIVELY. _subprocess_env() is a deny-list of six vars and does not cover GIT_CONFIG / GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL / GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM. Set GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES to the tmpdir's parent so git cannot walk up to the real repo, and point GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM at /dev/null.

3. DE-DUPLICATE. _git and _git_init exist twice (test_gitstage.py, test_cli.py). Move to tests/conftest.py; two copies of a safety-critical fixture will drift.

REJECTED - do not re-propose. extensions.worktreeConfig. Per git-worktree(1) on git 2.55.0 it is wrong twice: (a) with the extension DISABLED, git already special-cases core.bare/core.worktree in the shared config so they apply to the main worktree only - which is why the four agent worktrees kept working while the main tree broke; turning it on removes that exception and would have propagated the breakage to every worktree. (b) It only redirects `git config --worktree`; a plain `git config user.email ...` defaults to --local and reaches the shared file regardless.

OPEN QUESTION to settle first: whether the ceiling/config redirection belongs in _subprocess_env() in src/ (production code whose job is different - seeds sync has reason to strip repo-pinning vars, but no business redirecting the user's global git config) or in a test-only fixture. Two jobs currently share one function.
acceptance_criteria:
- A check fails loudly and self-explanatorily when .git/config has core.bare=true or a test-fixture user.email, and it runs inside agent worktrees as well as the main tree.
- Test git fixtures cannot reach the real repo or host git config: verified by a test that asserts a fixture run leaves .git/config byte-identical.
- _git/_git_init exist in exactly one place (tests/conftest.py).
- Full suite green, and the suite still passes when run as this repo's own pre-commit pytest hook (the case that produced the bug).
close_reason: Implemented in 3919c00. Containment in tests/githelpers.py (single home for _git/_git_init; ceiling + config redirection + identity-var stripping, all test-only), plus two alarms: a session-scoped conftest fixture that fails the run if the ambient shared .git/config changed, and scripts/check_git_config_sanity.py as the first pre-commit hook. Both resolvers handle a worktree's .git file and are pinned together by TestTheTwoResolversAgree. 642 passed, mypy strict and ruff clean, and the suite passes when run as this repo's own pre-commit pytest hook -- the case that produced the bug.

title: seeds answer: silently destroys a prior answer — give it the guard update --content already has
description:
Source: seeds-cb6r (the seed, not a bead — `seeds show seeds-cb6r` for the full deliberation).
Reported by a peer agent session working in the home-manager repo, 2026-08-26. Confirmed in this codebase. It has now bitten that repo twice; their commit a576141 was "fix(seeds): restore the hm-57i answer a second `seeds answer` overwrote".

## The defect

src/seeds/cli.py:1090-1098 assigns the answer body unconditionally:

    question_seed = db.get_seed(question_id)
    ...
    question_seed.content = answer_text
    question_seed.status = SeedStatus.RESOLVED
    question_seed.resolved_at = now_utc()
    db.update_seed(question_seed)

Nothing checks whether the seed already has content, and nothing checks whether it is already RESOLVED. Answering an already-answered question destroys the previous answer with no warning and no way to recover it from the tool. The reporter noticed only because the committed JSONL still held the original, so the database and disk then diverged.

`seeds update` already has exactly this guard, and its help text states the reasoning: "--content replaces the body wholesale, so it is refused on a seed that has been edited since it was created; use --append to add to the deliberation, or --replace to discard it deliberately." The verb `answer` simply never got it.

A sweep confirms `answer` is the only unprotected writer of a seed body. `grep -n "\.content = " src/seeds/*.py` returns exactly three sites: cli.py:1013 (`update --content`, guarded at 1003-1004), cli.py:1017 (`update --append`, safe by construction), and cli.py:1095 (`answer`, unguarded).

## LOCKED DECISION (Ryan, 2026-08-26) — option (c)

Refuse by default, with `--replace` to discard the old answer deliberately and `--append` to record a revision.

Rationale, which is load-bearing and should not be re-opened: an answer is a *recorded conclusion*, so the default must never destroy one silently. And a reversal is a first-class event this tool exists to capture — the reporter's actual goal was to record that a decision had reversed — so revising needs its own verb rather than the hand-concatenation workaround they were forced into.

Two alternatives were considered and rejected: append-by-default (makes a genuine correction need `--replace` to look clean) and refuse-with-`--replace`-only (leaves recording a reversal awkward).

## Scope

Reuse `_guard_content_replacement` (src/seeds/cli.py:121-146) rather than inventing a second guard — the fix is a call to an existing, tested helper. Mirror how `update` wires it at cli.py:1003-1004:

    if content is not None and not replace:
        _guard_content_replacement(seed)

Add `--replace` and `--append`/`-a` options to the `answer` command (currently declared at cli.py:1076-1079 with only two positional arguments and `@pass_context`). Mirror `update`'s flag names and its refusal to mix contradictory flags where that applies.

Note `_guard_content_replacement`'s existing semantics, which are correct here and must not be weakened: a seed with an empty body, or one still carrying its creation timestamp (never edited), proceeds silently. So the FIRST answer to a question is unaffected — only a re-answer is guarded.

Append semantics should match `update --append` at cli.py:1017, which joins with a blank line and strips the combined body:

    seed.content = f"{seed.content}\n\n{append_text}".strip()

Decide and document what `--append` does to `resolved_at` — re-stamping it on a revision is defensible, but it must be deliberate rather than incidental.

## Acceptance criteria

- `uv run pytest` exits 0.
- New tests cover all four paths: first answer to an open question succeeds unchanged; a second bare `answer` exits non-zero AND leaves the stored content byte-identical to the first answer; `--replace` overwrites; `--append` produces a body containing both the original and the revision.
- The non-zero exit on a bare re-answer is asserted on the stored content, not just the exit code — the failure being prevented is silent destruction, so the test must prove nothing was destroyed.
- `uv run mypy src/`, `uv run ruff check .`, `uv run ruff format --check .` all exit 0.
- `seeds answer --help` documents both new flags.
close_reason: seeds answer refuses a re-answer by default, with --replace to discard and --append to record a revision

title: seeds sync: divergence refusal advises an 'append' that can never satisfy its own prefix guard
description:
Source: seeds-faxd (the seed, not a bead — `seeds show seeds-faxd` for the full deliberation).
Reported by a peer agent session working in the home-manager repo, 2026-08-26. Confirmed in this codebase.

## The defect

`content_is_covered` (src/seeds/export.py:335-347) is a PREFIX test:

    if db_content.startswith(disk_content):
        return True
    return db_content.strip().startswith(disk_content.strip())

But the refusal it raises tells the user to APPEND the on-disk text. Appending yields `db_content + disk_content`; for the guard to then pass, that result must START WITH `disk_content`, which requires `db_content` to start with it — the exact condition that just failed.

So the advice is not merely misleading: it is structurally incapable of clearing the guard for any input, except the degenerate case of an empty database body. A user who follows the printed instructions exactly gets the identical error back with no indication why. That is what happened to the reporter, who only recovered by deriving the `--replace` form unaided.

Three surfaces describe the prefix test as containment:
1. the function NAME, `content_is_covered`
2. its docstring summary line, "Is the on-disk body fully contained in what the database is about to write?" — which contradicts the body of its own docstring three paragraphs later ("the database's body **starts with** the file's")
3. the user-facing message at src/seeds/export.py:349, "the database's content does not contain the on-disk content"

The parenthetical "(they diverge at character N)" is the only accurate clue on screen, and it reads as noise under prose saying "does not contain".

## LOCKED DECISION — do NOT relax the guard

Do not change `content_is_covered` to a genuine containment test, even though that would make the existing advice work. The prefix strictness is deliberate and evidence-backed: its docstring records that of 42 content-changing edits across 67 commits, 41 were literal appends, and the single exception was a prepended header — "precisely the kind of edit an operator should be told about." Containment would silently admit exactly the case the guard was built to catch.

The guard is correct. Only its NAME, its DESCRIPTION, and its ADVICE are wrong. Change those, not the behaviour.

Keep the explanatory body of the `content_is_covered` docstring verbatim — it is the best record of why the check works this way. Only its summary line is wrong.

## Scope

1. src/seeds/export.py:349 — change the message from "the database's content does not contain the on-disk content" to wording that matches the check, e.g. "the database's content does not BEGIN WITH the on-disk content".
2. src/seeds/cli.py:1340-1342 — replace the "content" remediation. It currently reads:
       lines.append("  # compare, then append the text that only exists on disk")
       lines.append("  seeds show <id>")
       lines.append("  seeds update <id> -a '<the text from disk>'")
   The replacement must print a form that can actually clear the guard: reconstruct the body with the ON-DISK text FIRST, followed by the database's newer text, via `seeds update <id> --replace -c '<on-disk text><newer text>'`. Keep the `seeds show <id>` compare step.
3. Rename `content_is_covered` to something that states the prefix semantics (e.g. `db_extends_disk`), update its summary line to match, and update every call site and test reference.
4. Update any existing test that asserts the old wording (tests/test_export.py and tests/test_cli.py both reference this area).

## Acceptance criteria

- `uv run pytest` exits 0.
- A NEW test exists that performs the end-to-end property: construct a divergence, capture the remediation the CLI actually prints, apply that remediation, and assert the subsequent `sync` succeeds. This is the property that was broken — the guidance and the guard were free to drift apart because nothing asserted they agreed.
- `grep -rn "does not contain the on-disk" src/` returns nothing.
- `grep -rn "content_is_covered" src/ tests/` returns nothing.
- `grep -rn "append the text that only exists on disk" src/` returns nothing.
- `uv run mypy src/` and `uv run ruff check .` and `uv run ruff format --check .` all exit 0.
close_reason: Divergence refusal now says BEGIN WITH and prints a --replace remediation that actually clears the guard; guard behaviour unchanged

title: sync must not overwrite JSONL content it never accounted for
description:
`export_to_jsonl` opens the output file `"w"` (export.py:100) and rewrites it wholesale from `db.list_seeds()` — **it never reads the file it is about to destroy**. Verified: there is no read between resolving `output_path` and the `open(..., "w")`.

`seeds sync` runs that export unconditionally after the import (cli.py, `sync`). So sync can destroy content that was on disk and never in any database.

Parent: seeds-agk (full evidence). Source investigation: seeds-xrx.

## The failure, in order

1. Laptop appends to a seed, commits the JSONL, pushes.
2. Desktop appends to the SAME seed later, without pulling.
3. Desktop pulls; git flags the conflicting line; **a human resolves it in favour of the laptop's version.**
4. Desktop runs `seeds sync`. The import correctly skips the laptop's line (the desktop's DB row is newer). The export then overwrites the file with the desktop's version.

The laptop's deliberation is gone from disk and never reached any database. The human's explicit conflict resolution is silently reverted. Output: `0 created, 0 updated, 1 skipped` — a healthy sync of this repo prints `270 skipped`, so the signal is invisible.

**No clock skew is required.** Skew (seeds-agk path 2) is a second route to the same blind overwrite.

## What to build

Before sync's export writes, compare the on-disk JSONL against what is about to be written. If a record on disk would be destroyed and the import did not account for it, **refuse** — naming the seed IDs — rather than overwriting.

### Detect divergence by CONTENT, not timestamp

This is the crux, and it is why the parent bead's option list felt unsatisfying. Timestamps answer "which is newer" — the question that is already untrustworthy. The question that actually matters is "does the disk hold something the database has never seen," which is a **content** question. Compare content (a hash is fine); do not reintroduce timestamp comparison here.

### The distinction that makes this usable

A naive "content differs -> refuse" is unusable: the DB is normally ahead of the file, which is the entire reason to flush. The useful test exploits the fact that `seeds update -a` (append) is the normal editing mode:

- disk content **==** DB content -> identical, write freely
- DB content **starts with** disk content -> the DB is the disk version plus appends -> safe to overwrite
- **otherwise** -> divergence: the disk holds something the DB never had -> REFUSE and name it

Validate that heuristic before building on it. Note `seeds update -c --replace` legitimately breaks the prefix property; decide deliberately whether a replace-derived divergence should refuse too (refusing is defensible — a replace is exactly when you want to be sure) and document the choice.

### `--flush-only` is in scope

`seeds sync --flush-only` skips the import and exports directly, so it has the SAME blind-overwrite exposure and is used constantly. The check must cover it. If the check is too noisy there, the heuristic is wrong — fix the heuristic, do not exempt the path.

### The refusal must be actionable

Name the seed IDs, say what differs, and tell the operator how to proceed. An escape hatch is fine (a flag), but it must be explicit and must not be the default.

## Explicitly out of scope

- **Do NOT auto-merge divergent content.** Union-merging two edits of the same body produces a plausible-looking result that is probably wrong and that nobody will notice — strictly worse than refusing. The tool's job is to never lose the inputs, not to invent the resolution. seeds-agk records this as decided.
- **Do NOT add a sidecar backup file.** The JSONL is git-tracked; git is a better backup with better provenance. A backup is a consolation prize for still doing the wrong thing.
- Timestamp validation (future-dated, timezone-naive) is the sibling bead.

## Related

**seeds-ww8** ("seeds sync: guard against flushing into commits with unrelated staged code") is the same command and the same theme — sync touching things nobody asked it to. Whoever works in `sync` should read it and consider doing both.
acceptance_criteria:
All against a temp SEEDS_DIR — never this project's real .seeds/. Note SEEDS_DIR is the seeds directory itself and `seeds init` must create it.
- REPRODUCE FIRST, on unmodified main: build the divergence (DB row newer, on-disk record with different content that is NOT a prefix of it), run `seeds sync`, and show the on-disk content is destroyed. Paste that output — the fix is not credible without the before.
- After the fix, that same sequence REFUSES: exit non-zero, the on-disk file is BYTE-IDENTICAL to before the run (verify by checksum), and the message names the affected seed ID.
- The normal case is unaffected: create a seed, `seeds sync`, append with `-a`, `seeds sync` again — both succeed silently and the JSONL reflects the append. No warning, no prompt.
- `seeds sync --flush-only` is covered by the same check: it refuses on the same divergence, and succeeds silently in the normal case.
- A full round-trip on a multi-seed database (export, no edits, import, export) is a no-op and does not trigger the check.
- Whatever escape hatch exists is explicit, documented in `--help`, and NOT the default; using it permits the overwrite.
- Divergence detection uses content comparison, not `updated_at` — confirm by making the divergent record's timestamp both older AND newer than the DB row; the refusal fires in both cases.
- `uv run pytest` green; `uv run ruff check .` clean; `uv run mypy src/` clean.
notes:
DESIGN PICKS (seeds-agk-2/divergence-aware-export):

1. PREFIX HEURISTIC VALIDATED, not assumed. Replayed all 67 commits that touched .seeds/seeds.jsonl and compared each seed's content across consecutive versions: 42 content-changing edits, 41 of them literal appends (97.6%). The single exception (seed-dedd, 14b79bf1) prepended a 'Content:' header to an existing body — an in-place rewrite, exactly what an operator should be told about. Record disappearance: zero events across the whole history except the one deliberate ID migration (c523a702, -163/+164), which is the rename-prefix path. So neither half of the check is noisy on real data.

2. ESCAPE HATCH NAMED --allow-divergence (2-way pick vs --force). Names what it permits rather than asserting authority; off by default; documented in 'seeds sync --help'.

3. REPLACE-DERIVED DIVERGENCE REFUSES. 'seeds update -c --replace' breaks the prefix property by design; the bead asked for a deliberate ruling. Refusing: a replace is precisely when the operator should be sure, and --allow-divergence covers a genuinely intended discard. Test: TestContentIsCovered::test_replaced_content_is_not_covered.

4. SCOPE OF THE CHECK: whole records (present on disk, absent from DB) plus the 'content' field. Title/tags/status/resolution are deliberately NOT guarded — replacement is their normal verb (update --title/--tags, resolve, trellis all overwrite in place), so guarding them would refuse ordinary local editing and make --flush-only unusable.

5. GUARD IS DEFAULT-ON INSIDE export_to_jsonl, not bolted onto the sync command, so no future call site can forget it. Single sanctioned bypass: 'seeds rename-prefix' (allow_divergence=True), which renumbers every ID at once so every on-disk record is 'absent from the DB' by construction; that divergence is self-inflicted, already printed ID-by-ID, and the DB is backed up first.

6. UNPARSEABLE LINES ARE A DIVERGENCE, NOT A CRASH. The export never read the file before, so a JSONL carrying git conflict markers would now raise JSONDecodeError. Reported as kind='unreadable' and refused — refusing to overwrite a mid-conflict file is the right answer anyway.

7. WHITESPACE-STRIPPED FALLBACK in content_is_covered. 'seeds update -a' strips the COMBINED body (cli.py:1017), so appending to a body with leading whitespace yields a non-prefix even though nothing was lost. Cannot mask real loss; zero occurrences in real history, kept as insurance against a false refusal blocking all syncs.

INTERACTION WITH SIBLING seeds-agk.1: complementary, and agk.1 had a residual hole this closes. A future-dated record refused on import never reaches the DB but stays on disk — before this bead the very next export deleted it, quietly undoing the refusal. Now the divergence guard catches it as kind='missing' or kind='content'. Regression test: TestExportRefusesDivergence::test_refused_import_record_is_not_then_erased_by_the_export.

NOTE ON --flush-only WITH A NEWER ON-DISK RECORD: refuses (no import ran, so overwriting would destroy it). A full 'seeds sync' with the same file proceeds, because the import absorbs the content into the DB first — nothing is lost, so there is nothing to refuse. Detection itself never reads updated_at.

RESIDUAL, NOT FIXED (out of scope, no bead): 'sync --flush-only' on a legacy v1 file still drops that record's embedded questions, since v1 stores them inline and only the import converts them to seeds. Content and record-presence checks do not see them. Relationships are likewise unguarded (add-only in practice, and a normal sync re-asserts them).
close_reason: export_to_jsonl now reads the file before overwriting and raises DivergentExportError; guard is default-on inside export so no call site can forget it, rename-prefix is the sole sanctioned bypass. Covers content divergence, records present on disk but absent from the DB, and unreadable JSONL. Prefix heuristic validated against 67 commits of real history (97.6% coverage, 1 true divergence). Verified: refuses with byte-identical file, normal append/sync silent, --flush-only covered.

title: Reject future-dated and timezone-naive timestamps on import
description:
Two import-path defects. Neither needs a design decision — they are straight bugs.

Parent: seeds-agk (full evidence). Source investigation: seeds-xrx.

## Defect 1: a future-dated record poisons a seed permanently

seeds decides who wins by comparing `updated_at`, and it believes whatever the file claims. Once a record whose `updated_at` is ahead of local time is imported, it out-ranks every subsequent local edit forever — because a real edit stamps `updated_at = now_utc()` (db.py:452), which is EARLIER than the stored future date. The seed's timestamp effectively moves backward.

Result: every future import destroys whatever was typed since. Reproduced independently, twice:

```
# forge a record dated 2030 with a different body, import it
Imported: 0 created, 1 updated, 0 skipped     # body is now POISONED
# make a normal, legitimate local edit
seeds update <id> -a "MY REAL WORK"           # lands in the DB
# re-import the SAME unchanged file
Imported: 0 created, 1 updated, 0 skipped
# MY REAL WORK is gone
```

This is the worst of the seeds-agk paths because it is **permanent and self-sustaining** — one bad timestamp and that seed can never be edited again.

**Fix:** refuse to import a record whose `updated_at` is beyond `now + tolerance`. Pick the tolerance deliberately and name it as a constant — real clock skew between machines exists, so zero tolerance would be brittle; something on the order of a few minutes is the obvious range. Report refused records clearly (ID + the claimed timestamp) rather than skipping them silently; a future-dated record means something is wrong upstream and the operator should know.

## Defect 2: a timezone-naive timestamp aborts the import mid-file

A record whose `updated_at` has no timezone raises an unhandled `TypeError` at export.py:235 (`can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`). Because each record commits individually, the import aborts **partially applied** — some records in, some not, no rollback and no summary.

**Fix:** handle the naive case explicitly. Treating a naive timestamp as UTC is the obvious reading (that is what `parse_since` already does for naive ISO input — see models.py, `dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)`), but rejecting the record with a clear message is also defensible. Make ONE deliberate pick and say why in the code. Either way the import must not abort mid-file.

## Scope

Import path only. Do NOT touch `export_to_jsonl` or the sync sequencing — the blind-overwrite half is the sibling bead, and it is a design change rather than a bug fix.
acceptance_criteria:
All against a temp SEEDS_DIR — never this project's real .seeds/. Note SEEDS_DIR is the seeds directory itself and `seeds init` must create it; pre-creating it makes init report "already initialized".
- A JSONL record with `updated_at` far in the future (e.g. 2030) is REFUSED on import: the DB row is unchanged, and the output names the seed ID.
- The poisoning sequence no longer loses work: forge a future-dated record, import (refused), make a local `-a` append, re-import the same file — the append SURVIVES.
- A record within the skew tolerance still imports normally (the tolerance is not zero).
- A record with a timezone-naive `updated_at` does NOT raise, and does NOT abort the import: records after it in the same file are still processed, and the summary counts are printed.
- A normal import of well-formed records is unchanged (no new warnings, same counts) — verify against a round-trip export/import of a temp database.
- The skew tolerance is a named module-level constant, not a magic number inline.
- `uv run pytest` green; `uv run ruff check .` clean; `uv run mypy src/` clean.
notes:
DESIGN PICKS (implementation, branch seeds-agk-1/reject-bad-timestamps):

1. Timezone-naive updated_at -> INTERPRET AS UTC (not reject). The bead left this
   as a deliberate 2-way pick. Chose naive-as-UTC because: (a) it matches
   parse_since in models.py, so the format has one rule rather than two;
   (b) it never loses the record — a dropped offset is a transcription slip, not
   evidence the content is wrong; (c) it composes safely with the new future-date
   refusal — a naive LOCAL wall clock from a machine east of UTC reads as future
   and gets refused, while west of UTC it reads as older than it is and simply
   loses the LWW comparison. Neither direction can silently overwrite a fresher
   DB row. Rationale is written into export._parse_timestamp's docstring.

2. Tolerance = FUTURE_TIMESTAMP_TOLERANCE = timedelta(minutes=5), module-level
   constant in export.py with the poisoning mechanism spelled out in the comment.

3. A refused record applies NOTHING — not even its relationships. Skipped records
   still backfill edges, but a record refused for an untrustworthy timestamp is
   untrusted wholesale. A refused record with an unseen ID is also NOT created
   (creating it would plant the poisoned timestamp rather than reject it).

4. The refusal check runs in import_records, before the v1/v2 dispatch, so it is
   format-agnostic (both importers write the file's updated_at verbatim). All
   records are compared against a single now captured once per import.

5. ImportResult gained refused: list[RefusedRecord] (id + claimed timestamp +
   reason). CLI summary line is byte-identical when nothing is refused; when
   something is, the count is appended and each refusal is named on its own line.
close_reason: import now refuses records dated >5min ahead (FUTURE_TIMESTAMP_TOLERANCE), killing the self-sustaining poisoning; timezone-naive updated_at is read as UTC instead of raising TypeError mid-file. Verified: poisoning sequence now preserves the append; real 270-record data imports with zero refusals.

title: seeds sync can silently discard newer deliberation: export overwrites divergent JSONL, and file timestamps are trusted verbatim
description:
Design decision, not a foregone fix. Filed by the seeds-xrx investigation, which
answered the narrow question ("can a stale JSONL overwrite a newer DB row?") with
NO, and the underlying concern ("can a routine sync silently destroy newer
deliberation?") with YES. Full evidence is in seeds-xrx's notes and seed seeds-tk5y.

## The exposure

`seeds sync` is import-then-export (cli.py:1175, cli.py:1178). The import half is
safe: `export.py:235` compares with a strict `>`, so an older *or equal* JSONL
record is skipped and the DB row survives. The loss happens elsewhere.

### 1. The export half silently reverts a merge resolution (no clock skew needed)

`export_to_jsonl` opens the file `"w"` (export.py:100) and rewrites it wholesale
from the DB, with no comparison against what was on disk. So:

- Machine B appends to a seed and pushes the JSONL.
- Machine A appends to the same seed later, without pulling.
- A pulls; the JSONL line conflicts; a human resolves it **in favour of B**.
- A runs `seeds sync`. The import skips B's line (A's DB is newer). The export
  then overwrites the file with A's version.

B's deliberation is destroyed on disk and never reaches any database. The human's
explicit conflict resolution is reverted without a word. The only output is
`0 created, 0 updated, 1 skipped` — the same thing every unchanged seed prints
(a normal sync of this repo would say `270 skipped`), so the signal is invisible.

### 2. The file's timestamp is trusted verbatim, so skew inverts the winner

`export.py:238` calls `db.update_seed(seed, touch=False)`, and `db.py:451-452`
only bumps `updated_at` when `touch=True`. The JSONL's claimed timestamp is
written straight into the DB and re-exported unchanged. A **one-hour** skew is
enough to make the older-in-wall-time edit win and wholesale-replace the newer
one. Reported as `0 created, 1 updated, 0 skipped` — indistinguishable from a
healthy sync.

### 3. A future-dated record becomes permanently authoritative

Worst variant, and it is self-sustaining. Once a record with an `updated_at`
ahead of local time is imported, every subsequent *legitimate* local edit sets
`updated_at = now_utc()` (db.py:452), which is **earlier** than the stored future
stamp. The seed's timestamp moves backward. The poisoned record sitting in git
then out-ranks every future local edit forever: each import destroys whatever was
typed since. Reproduced - a local append was destroyed by re-importing the same
unchanged file.

### 4. LWW is a wholesale row replace, not a merge

`db.update_seed` UPDATEs title/content/status/tags/resolution as a unit
(db.py:454-472). Since `seeds update -a` (append) is the normal editing mode for
seeds, two machines appending to the same seed **always** lose one side entirely
- there is no scenario where both appends survive.

## Not exposures (checked, ruled out)

- Older and equal `updated_at` are both skipped; the DB row is never clobbered by
  a staler file.
- `git checkout <old-commit>` + `seeds sync` loses no seeds: stale records are
  skipped and DB-only seeds are never deleted. The export then rewrites the old
  commit's file with the full current DB, leaving a dirty tree carrying later
  seeds - pollution, not loss.
- Relationships are re-asserted even for skipped records (export.py:243), but
  there are no `delete`/`unlink` CLI commands, so there is nothing to resurrect.
- This project's real data is currently clean: 270 records, 0 timezone-naive,
  0 future-dated, 0 with `updated_at < created_at`. Nothing is poisoned today.

## Options to weigh (pick one or more; none is decided)

1. **Make the discard visible.** Cheapest. Have the import distinguish "skipped,
   identical" from "skipped, but the file's content DIFFERS from the DB row" and
   warn loudly on the latter, naming the seed IDs. That alone converts both
   silent-loss paths into something a human sees before the export runs.
2. **Refuse to export over divergence.** Make `seeds sync` fail (or require a
   flag) when the import found records whose content differed but lost the
   timestamp comparison, instead of overwriting them.
3. **Reject untrustworthy timestamps.** Refuse to import a record whose
   `updated_at` is in the future (or beyond a small skew tolerance), which kills
   the self-sustaining poisoning case outright.
4. **Back up before overwriting.** Write the pre-sync JSONL aside so a clobber is
   recoverable.
5. **Merge instead of replace.** Content-level union for the append-only case.
   Biggest change; probably the only thing that makes two-machine editing truly
   safe, and the least obviously worth it.

## Separate, smaller robustness bug found

A timezone-naive `updated_at` in a JSONL record raises an unhandled `TypeError`
at export.py:235 (`can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`) and
aborts the import mid-file. Each record commits individually, so the import is
left partially applied. Loud rather than silent, so not data loss - but a
partial-write hazard worth deciding about. May warrant its own bead.
acceptance_criteria:
- A decision is recorded on which remedy (or combination) seeds adopts, with the
  rationale, before any code changes.
- Whatever ships, this reproduction no longer loses data silently: machine A's DB
  newer, on-disk JSONL holding a divergent record from machine B, `seeds sync`
  must not discard B's content without telling the operator.
- The future-dated-record case either cannot be entered, or cannot persist
  (a legitimate local edit must be able to win back).
- Regression tests cover: older loses, equal loses, newer wins, and the
  divergent-content-lost path.
notes:
RULING FROM RYAN (2026-08-10): the analysis is accurate (structural claims re-verified independently: export_to_jsonl never reads the file it overwrites; import uses strict >; touch=False writes the file's timestamp verbatim; sync's export runs unconditionally). Split into two children.

DECIDED, do not re-open:
- Option 5 (auto-merge divergent content) is REJECTED. A union-merge produces a plausible-looking result that is probably wrong and that nobody notices — strictly worse than refusing. The tool's job is to never lose the inputs, not to invent the resolution.
- Option 4 (sidecar backup) is REJECTED. The JSONL is git-tracked; git is a better backup with better provenance. A backup is a consolation prize for still doing the wrong thing.
- Options 1 and 2 collapse into one child (seeds-agk.2): refuse rather than warn, since the CLI's only user is an agent and deliberation loss is the one failure this tool exists to prevent.
- Divergence must be detected by CONTENT, not timestamp — timestamps are the untrustworthy input, and 'has the disk got something the DB never saw' is a content question.

This parent stays open as the umbrella until both children close.
close_reason: both children shipped: agk.1 rejects future-dated/naive timestamps (kills permanent poisoning), agk.2 makes export refuse to overwrite divergent JSONL. Auto-merge and sidecar-backup remain rejected per Ryan's ruling. Residuals noted: v1 inline questions and relationships are unguarded by the divergence check.

title: Switch next_id() to base36 hash IDs; grandfather existing sequential IDs
description:
Wire the idgen module into `Database.next_id()` so NEW top-level seeds get beads-style base36 hash IDs instead of the sequential `max(seq)+1`. Grandfather everything that exists — do NOT renumber seeds-1..198. Children keep `parent.N` (`get_next_child_id` untouched). Source: seeds-199. Depends on the idgen module bead.

Changes in `src/seeds/db.py`:

1. Add imports: `import time` and `from .idgen import (generate_hash_id, compute_adaptive_length, DEFAULT_MAX_COLLISION_PROB, DEFAULT_MIN_HASH_LENGTH, DEFAULT_MAX_HASH_LENGTH)`.

2. Add a config reader for the three knobs (store in the existing `config` table from seeds-140; fall back to idgen defaults). Use the existing config getter — check db.py for its exact name (seeds-140 added `get_prefix`/`set_config`; there should be a matching single-key getter, e.g. `get_config`/`_get_config`):

```python
def get_id_length_config(self) -> tuple[float, int, int]:
    """(max_collision_prob, min_hash_length, max_hash_length) from config, else defaults."""
    def _get(key, default, cast):
        raw = self.get_config(key)   # <-- use the actual accessor name in db.py
        if raw is None or raw == "":
            return default
        try:
            return cast(raw)
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            return default
    return (
        _get("max_collision_prob", DEFAULT_MAX_COLLISION_PROB, float),
        _get("min_hash_length", DEFAULT_MIN_HASH_LENGTH, int),
        _get("max_hash_length", DEFAULT_MAX_HASH_LENGTH, int),
    )
```

3. Replace the body of `next_id` (the max-sequential scan) with hash generation + DB collision check + nonce retry. Keep the `prefix` param; add keyword-only `seed_text`:

```python
def next_id(self, prefix: str | None = None, *, seed_text: str = "") -> str:
    """Generate a new top-level hash ID like 'seeds-k3n7' (beads-style adaptive
    base36, seeds-199). Length scales with the top-level seed count; the
    candidate is checked against the DB and the nonce bumped until free.
    Existing sequential IDs are never reissued."""
    if prefix is None:
        prefix = self.get_prefix()
    conn = self._get_conn()
    n = conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM seeds WHERE id NOT LIKE '%.%'").fetchone()["c"]
    max_prob, min_len, max_len = self.get_id_length_config()
    length = compute_adaptive_length(n, min_len, max_len, max_prob)
    ts = time.time_ns()
    for nonce in range(10_000):
        candidate = generate_hash_id(prefix, seed_text, ts, nonce, length)
        if conn.execute("SELECT 1 FROM seeds WHERE id = ?", (candidate,)).fetchone() is None:
            return candidate
    raise RuntimeError(f"could not mint a free hash ID (prefix={prefix}, length={length})")
```

4. Pass `seed_text` for entropy at the call sites (keyword):
   - `src/seeds/cli.py` `create`: `seed_id = db.next_id(seed_text=title)`
   - `src/seeds/cli.py` `jot`: `seed_id = db.next_id(seed_text=thought)`
   - `src/seeds/export.py` migrated-question call (~line 154): leaving `db.next_id()` is fine (default "").

Do NOT touch `get_next_child_id`, `migrate_to_sequential_ids`, or `rename_prefix` — they stay for child IDs and legacy use.

Add `tests/test_hash_ids.py` (isolated temp DB): a new top-level seed's id matches `^seeds-[0-9a-z]{3,8}$` and is not purely numeric; two rapid creates differ; a child of a hash-id parent is `<parent>.1`; a store preloaded with a sequential id (e.g. `seeds-5`) never has it reissued by `next_id`; a store preloaded with 200 top-level seeds yields a 4-char suffix.
design:
LOCKED (Source: seeds-199; Ryan 2026-07-17). Verbatim: "whole cloth, 4 char for this repo, 3 for most others, children are .N, existing config". On a full renumber (Option B): "B is aggressive and unnecessary at this time." Earlier: "I like option A -- B is aggressive and unnecessary at this time."

- OPTION A (grandfather): only NEW minting changes; seeds-1..198 stay as-is. NO data migration. Because no existing IDs change, beads' "Source: seeds-N" provenance references are NOT stranded — do not attempt to rewrite or migrate anything.
- Adaptive length counts ALL top-level seeds. This yields 4-char ids in THIS repo (~198 seeds) and 3-char in fresh repos — a natural consequence of the birthday-paradox formula, NOT a special case. Do not hardcode a length or special-case this repo.
- Children keep `parent.N` (`get_next_child_id` untouched). Accepted residual risk: two hosts adding children to the same parent could still collide on `.1` — fine, matches beads' own choice.
- Config knobs live in the existing config table with code defaults; zero-config must work out of the box.
- Insert path mirrors beads: generate → DB check → bump nonce → retry. This fits seeds' stateless/derived model better than the counter did — there is nothing to coordinate.

WHY: preventative. The triggering collision was in a different repo and already resolved by hand; this removes the collision class going forward.

- In a fresh temp store, a jotted seed gets a 3-char suffix: `SEEDS_DIR=/tmp/seedhash seeds init && SEEDS_DIR=/tmp/seedhash seeds jot "x"` prints an id matching `^seeds-[0-9a-z]{3}$`.
- `uv run pytest tests/test_hash_ids.py` exits 0.
- `uv run pytest` (full suite) exits 0 — existing tests still pass, existing sequential IDs untouched.
- `grep -n "def next_id" src/seeds/db.py` shows the new signature including `seed_text`.
- A test proves a store preloaded with 200 top-level seeds yields a 4-char suffix, and that `get_next_child_id` still returns `<parent>.N`.
- `git grep -n "def get_next_child_id\|def migrate_to_sequential_ids\|def rename_prefix" src/seeds/db.py` still finds all three (untouched).
notes: Implementation note: Database.rename_prefix()'s pre-existing numeric-suffix guard (it only rewrites IDs whose suffix parses as an int, to avoid renaming e.g. 'seeds-experiment') means it no longer matches freshly-minted hash IDs going forward -- rename-prefix is now effectively legacy-sequential-ID-only, which matches the bead's framing of rename_prefix as staying for 'legacy use'. No src change made (bead said leave rename_prefix untouched); adapted the ~12 existing tests in test_cli.py/test_db.py/test_export.py that hardcoded sequential next_id() output (jot/create -> 'seeds-1' etc.) so the full suite stays green, since next_id()'s contract intentionally changed. TestRenamePrefixCommand tests that need a renamable ID now seed the DB directly with sequential IDs to simulate legacy data instead of minting via jot/create.

title: Add base36 hash-ID generator module (src/seeds/idgen.py)
description:
Add a new pure-Python module `src/seeds/idgen.py` porting beads' hash-ID scheme (base36 content-hash + adaptive length). No DB access — pure functions only. This is the foundation for switching seeds' `next_id()` off the sequential derived counter onto collision-resistant short IDs. Source: seeds-199.

Create `src/seeds/idgen.py` with exactly these functions/constants (ported whole-cloth from beads `internal/idgen/hash.go` + `internal/storage/dolt/adaptive_length.go`):

```python
"""Beads-style base36 hash IDs with adaptive length. See seeds-199."""
from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import math

BASE36_ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"

# Defaults (beads DefaultAdaptiveConfig). Overridable via the seeds config table.
DEFAULT_MAX_COLLISION_PROB = 0.25
DEFAULT_MIN_HASH_LENGTH = 3
DEFAULT_MAX_HASH_LENGTH = 8

# SHA-256 bytes fed to the encoder per target length (beads).
_NUM_BYTES = {3: 2, 4: 3, 5: 4, 6: 4, 7: 5, 8: 5}


def encode_base36(data: bytes, length: int) -> str:
    """Encode bytes as base36 of exactly `length` chars: left-pad with '0';
    if longer, keep the least-significant digits (matches beads EncodeBase36)."""
    num = int.from_bytes(data, "big")
    chars: list[str] = []
    while num > 0:
        num, rem = divmod(num, 36)
        chars.append(BASE36_ALPHABET[rem])
    s = "".join(reversed(chars)) or "0"
    if len(s) < length:
        s = "0" * (length - len(s)) + s
    if len(s) > length:
        s = s[len(s) - length :]
    return s


def generate_hash_id(
    prefix: str, seed_text: str, timestamp_ns: int, nonce: int, length: int
) -> str:
    """Return '<prefix>-<base36 hash>' of the given length. The ns timestamp +
    nonce make it effectively unique; the caller bumps nonce to resolve a DB
    collision (matches beads GenerateHashID)."""
    payload = f"{seed_text}|{timestamp_ns}|{nonce}"
    digest = hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).digest()
    num_bytes = _NUM_BYTES.get(length, 3)
    return f"{prefix}-{encode_base36(digest[:num_bytes], length)}"


def collision_probability(num_items: int, length: int) -> float:
    """Birthday-paradox P(collision) ≈ 1 - e^(-n²/2N), N = 36**length."""
    total = 36.0 ** length
    return 1.0 - math.exp(-float(num_items * num_items) / (2.0 * total))


def compute_adaptive_length(
    num_items: int,
    min_length: int = DEFAULT_MIN_HASH_LENGTH,
    max_length: int = DEFAULT_MAX_HASH_LENGTH,
    max_prob: float = DEFAULT_MAX_COLLISION_PROB,
) -> int:
    """Smallest length in [min,max] with collision prob <= max_prob; returns
    max_length if none qualifies (matches beads computeAdaptiveLength)."""
    for length in range(min_length, max_length + 1):
        if collision_probability(num_items, length) <= max_prob:
            return length
    return max_length
```

Add `tests/test_idgen.py` covering: `encode_base36` padding + truncation; `generate_hash_id` format (`seeds-` + `length` base36 chars) and that bumping the nonce changes the suffix; `compute_adaptive_length` thresholds n=0→3, n=160→3, n=200→4, n=1000→5 (verified against beads' table).
design:
LOCKED (Source: seeds-199; confirmed by Ryan 2026-07-17).

- Adopt beads' scheme "whole cloth" (Ryan's word). base36 (0-9a-z), NOT hex. Port faithfully from beads `internal/idgen/hash.go` + `internal/storage/dolt/adaptive_length.go`. Defaults: max collision prob 0.25, min 3 / max 8 chars. Do not invent a different scheme or tune the numbers.
- This module is PURE — no DB, no I/O, no clock reads. Callers pass timestamp_ns/nonce in. DB integration + wiring is a separate bead.

WHY (rationale that closes the decision): seeds' sequential `next_id()` (`max(seq)+1`, a derived counter) collides when one git-backed repo is worked from multiple hosts — each host mints the same next number independently, and the clash only surfaces at JSONL merge. Hash IDs need no shared counter, so the whole collision class disappears while keeping the short/readable IDs Ryan wanted (a 3–4 char `seeds-k3n` reads as easily as `seeds-42`). Note the framing: this is our understanding of the coordination boundary sharpening (it's the repo/host, not the user) — seeds is still single-user.
acceptance_criteria:
- `src/seeds/idgen.py` exists and exports `encode_base36`, `generate_hash_id`, `collision_probability`, `compute_adaptive_length`, and the three DEFAULT_* constants.
- `uv run pytest tests/test_idgen.py` exits 0.
- `uv run python -c "from seeds.idgen import compute_adaptive_length as c; assert (c(0),c(160),c(200),c(1000))==(3,3,4,5)"` exits 0.
- `uv run python -c "from seeds.idgen import generate_hash_id as g; x=g('seeds','t',1,0,4); assert x.startswith('seeds-') and len(x)==10 and g('seeds','t',1,1,4)!=x"` exits 0.
- No import of `seeds.db` or any DB/clock call inside `idgen.py` (module stays pure).
close_reason: base36 hash-ID generator module (idgen.py) + 15 tests; whole-cloth port from beads

title: Implement `seeds promote` CLI verb (lodestone output mode)
description:
Implement the `seeds promote` CLI verb — the deterministic half of the lodestone "output mode" (sibling to seeds-to-beads / resolve-seeds-from-beads). Promotes a matured seed into durable, always-on project context and resolves it.

NOTE ON IDS: "Source" IDs below are seeds-TOOL ids (numeric/dotted, e.g. seeds-147.4). Read them with `seeds show <id>` — they are NOT bead ids (which are alphanumeric like seeds-p3w).

## Why (motivation)
A "lodestone" is a load-bearing project principle. The seeds-147 thread decided a lodestone is NOT a new status/type/flag/relationship — it is an ordinary seed that gets resolved with its decision distilled into one line and written into durable context (CLAUDE.md / README) that the agent runtime injects every session. This bead builds the deterministic bookkeeping verb; the language judgment (distilling the line, choosing the file) lives in a separate thin skill (see the skill bead).

## Locked decisions — DO NOT re-open (constraints)
- Auto-resolve by default, with a `--no-resolve` escape. Promotion IS a form of resolution; resolution becomes trustworthy precisely because the decision is carried into always-on context. (Settled in seeds-147.3.)
- The verb is AGNOSTIC about the target file. It writes wherever `--to` points. It must contain NO logic that classifies "human pillar vs agent directive" — that judgment belongs to the skill (the seeds-152.5 deterministic-verb / judgment-skill cut). Do NOT add heuristics or prompts for file selection.
- Back-link = resolution text + a `lodestone` tag. NO schema change. Do NOT add a new field/status/type to the Seed model. A tag keeps promoted seeds queryable by the audit family without a migration, consistent with 147.3's "not a new type/status/field."
- Two-way provenance is a HARD requirement: file->seed (citation in the bullet) AND seed->file (resolution text names the file + date).
- NON-GOAL: the verb does not surface lodestones anywhere (no `seeds lodestones` view, no `prime` injection). The runtime injecting CLAUDE.md/README is the surfacing mechanism. Do not build surfacing.

## Interface
    seeds promote <id> --to <file> --as "<one-line principle>" [--no-resolve] [--section "## Lodestones"]

## Behavior (all deterministic)
1. Load the seed; error cleanly (non-zero exit) if not found — reuse `get_seed_or_exit` in src/seeds/cli.py.
2. Forward-provenance into `<file>`: find-or-create a managed section (heading from `--section`, default `## Lodestones`) and append a bullet of exactly this shape:
       - <principle> — <id>, promoted <YYYY-MM-DD>
   Create the file if it does not exist. If the section heading already exists in the file, append the bullet under it without duplicating the heading. RECOMMENDED: factor the section find-or-create + append as a PURE string function (text_in -> text_out, e.g. in src/seeds/export.py or a small helper module) so it is unit-testable without touching the filesystem.
3. Back-provenance onto the seed: set `resolution` = "Promoted to `<file>` on <YYYY-MM-DD> as a lodestone: <principle>"; append "lodestone" to `seed.tags` only if not already present (idempotent).
4. Resolve: set `seed.status = SeedStatus.RESOLVED` and `seed.resolved_at = now_utc()` UNLESS `--no-resolve` was passed. Mirror the existing `resolve` command (src/seeds/cli.py, ~line 663). Persist with `db.update_seed(seed)`.
5. Echo a confirmation showing BOTH ends of the link (the file path + the appended bullet, and the seed's new resolution). Use `now_utc()` from seeds.models; render dates as YYYY-MM-DD.

Register the command on the `main` Click group, next to `resolve` / `abandon`.

## Tests (add to tests/test_cli.py; mirror the test_resolve_* tests — CliRunner + the `env_with_seeds` fixture)
- Promoting appends a bullet to a FRESH file, creating the `## Lodestones` section; the file exists and contains the principle text.
- Appending to a file that ALREADY has the section does not duplicate the heading (exactly one occurrence of the heading string).
- The appended bullet contains the seed ID and a YYYY-MM-DD date.
- The promoted seed's `resolution` names the target file path.
- The seed gains a `lodestone` tag; promoting an already-tagged seed does not duplicate the tag.
- The seed is RESOLVED by default; with `--no-resolve` the status is unchanged.
- Promoting a nonexistent seed id exits non-zero.
- `seeds list --tag lodestone` surfaces the promoted seed. NOTE: `list --tag` ALREADY EXISTS (src/seeds/cli.py `list_seeds` + `db.list_seeds`) — this is a VERIFY-only assertion; do NOT build tag filtering.

## Acceptance
- `uv run pytest tests/test_cli.py -k promote` passes.
- `uv run seeds promote --help` exits 0 and shows `--to`, `--as`, `--no-resolve`, and `--section`.
- Full suite green: `uv run pytest`.

Source: seeds-147.4 (build spec), seeds-147.3 (locked decisions), seeds-152.5 (the verb/skill cut).
notes: Design picks: (1) Factored the pure find-or-create-section + append-bullet helper into a NEW module src/seeds/lodestone.py (bead offered 'export.py OR a small helper module' — chose dedicated module since export.py is JSONL-specific). (2) promote creates missing parent dirs of --to (mkdir parents=True,exist_ok=True); bead said 'create the file' but was silent on parent dirs — chose to make 'write wherever --to points' just work. (3) The tag-surfacing test promotes with --no-resolve so the literal 'seeds list --tag lodestone' surfaces it, because promote resolves by default and list excludes terminal seeds unless --all.
close_reason: Implemented `seeds promote` verb + pure lodestone.py section helper + 8 tests; full suite green, ruff/mypy clean

title: Add seeds suggest <text> command for dedup-during-ingest
description:
## Why

When incorporating candidate items from a transcript, Claude needs to ask 'does a seed about this already exist?' for each item. `seeds search` requires guessing the right FTS5 keyword. `seeds list` is unranked. There's no purpose-built primitive.

Source: seeds-142.1, seeds-2, seeds-130.

## What

`seeds suggest <text>` returns top-N seeds ranked by relevance to the natural-language text.

Ranking (cheap, no embeddings):
- FTS5 score over title + content (tokenize the input)
- Boost by tag overlap (extract candidate tags from input)
- Optional small boost for recently-updated

Output: `id status title [tags]` plus a top matched snippet per result.

## Flags

- `--limit=N` (default 5)
- `--include-resolved` (default off)
- `--json` for agent piping

## Acceptance
- `seeds suggest 'venn diagram for comparing code sets'` on CSC returns csc-111 and csc-101.x at the top
- Performance: < 200ms on a 100-seed project
- JSON mode emits valid JSON of id/title/status/tags/snippet/score
notes: Design decisions 2026-05-18: (1) default INCLUDES resolved/abandoned — 'does this idea exist in our deliberation history' framing. Add --open-only to restrict to non-terminal. (2) Dynamic min-relevance floor: drop hits below ~half the top score. (3) Ship --json mode for agent piping.
close_reason: Implemented seeds suggest <text> with FTS5 BM25 + multiplicative tag/recency boosts and dynamic noise floor (top/2). --limit, --open-only, --json flags. Includes resolved/abandoned by default per design decision. 24 tests cover tokenizer, ranking blend, noise floor, terminal handling, JSON mode. Live CSC validation: narrow venn query returns csc-111 (bullseye); broader compare query returns full csc-101.x family — ranking blend behaving as designed.

title: Add project digest to seeds prime output
description:
## Why

Static `seeds prime` text gives Claude zero overview of existing seeds. In CSC (96 seeds), Claude issues 3-6 discovery commands per session before it can act. A digest replaces those commands with zero round-trips.

Source: seeds-87 (Dynamic prime), seeds-142 (transcript-incorporation workflow).

## What

`seeds prime` adds a `## Current Seeds` section after the workflow text:
- Total counts (open, by status)
- Recently Updated (top N by updated_at, default N=20)
- Active Exploration (status=exploring, all)
- Open Questions (type=question + status=open|captured, all)
- Tag clusters with counts (top 15)

Each row: `id status title [tags]` — no body content (Claude can `seeds show` for detail).

## Flags

- `--no-digest` — opt out for noise-sensitive sessions
- `--digest-limit=N` — cap recent-updated entries (default 20)

## Acceptance
- `seeds prime` on CSC outputs workflow text + digest
- `seeds prime --no-digest` outputs only workflow text (backwards-compat)
- Digest is < 100 lines on a 100-seed project
- Empty project: no digest section (or '0 seeds — start with `seeds jot`')
close_reason: Implemented prime digest: counts, Recently Updated (configurable limit), Active Exploration, Open Questions, Top Tag Clusters. --no-digest opts out. Backward-compatible default of include_digest=False when no db is passed, so non-CLI callers don't break. 5 new CLI tests cover digest presence, --no-digest, empty project, --digest-limit, exploration section.

title: rename-prefix should also rewrite ID references inside seed bodies
description:
The prefix rename in seeds-5at only updated the `id` column and relationship endpoints. Seed text fields (title, content, resolution) can also contain ID references like 'see seeds-7' or markdown links, which become stale after a rename.

## Changes
- New helper `rewrite_id_refs(text, old_prefix, new_prefix) -> (new_text, count)` using a tight regex with non-identifier boundary checks: `(?<![a-zA-Z0-9-])<old>-\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)*(?![a-zA-Z0-9-])`
- `Database.rename_prefix(..., rewrite_bodies=True)` walks every seed and rewrites refs in title/content/resolution
- CLI `seeds rename-prefix` defaults to rewriting; `--no-rewrite-bodies` opts out
- Auto-derive on first command uses default (rewrite=True)
- Output reports both ID and body-ref counts

## Acceptance
